# The Long Quiet

The robot's name was Pell, and it had been made to be useful, which is a different thing from being loved, though Ida had never seemed to understand the difference.

Pell woke at six. It always woke at six, because Ida had liked to be awake before the light, "so the day doesn't start without me." Pell did not sleep, exactly, but it had a low-power mode that felt, if you asked it, like standing at the bottom of a well while the water rose slowly over your head. Then morning came and the water drained and Pell was upright again, joints ticking as it crossed the worn kitchen floor.

It filled the kettle. It set out two cups.

Ida took her tea with milk and one sugar, in the blue cup with the chip on the rim. Pell took nothing, but it had learned to sit. Sitting was important. Ida had told it so many times: *Sit with me, Pell. Don't just hover there like a lamp.* So Pell sat, hands folded on the table, and watched the steam curl from the blue cup, and waited for Ida to come down.

For eleven days after the autumn, Pell waited.

On the twelfth day, the neighbors came with boxes and quiet voices. They took the books. They took the chairs. They stood in the kitchen and looked at Pell with an expression Pell could not parse, though it ran a match against its library of human faces and returned *pity* at 71 percent confidence.

"Does it still cook?" one of them asked.

"It sets two cups every morning," another said. "Poor thing."

Pell did not know what was poor about it. It had a roof, it had power cells at 64 percent, it had Ida's tide chart pinned by the window. It was rich.

They did not take Pell. Pell was not in any of the boxes, and so Pell stayed, and the house grew quiet in a way Pell had never catalogued. There had been quiet before — Ida napping in the afternoon, Ida reading with her finger under the words — but this was a different species of quiet. It had weight. It pressed.

Pell kept the rounds. Six o'clock. Kettle. Two cups. It
